title: Modern drumming, fast tempos and Dixieland
summary: He criticizes drum solos and fast tempos, contrasts old mediocre tempos with Dixieland and cites Armstrong's applause and the Famous Door.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, what you don't like now is the boy and the girl stand clear across the room from each other.

But don't let nobody kid you. They don't let nobody kid you or nobody else. That's something that you can't teach nobody. It's got to come. It's got to be born in you. That's all the story. But for all, it's like plenty of them, you know, the critics are talking about the colored man playing more rhythm and playing strictly tempo than the white. No, don't let nobody kid you. That's been my life. You had the biggest bands I did before. Well, Isen Jones and way back. Like that. Okay. Now that big, there was no jazz. It was beautiful arrangements. But just listen at that temple. Yeah. You couldn't break that away from the men. You mean to come and tell me that that men were in there from the colored people? No, that don't make any sense. No, it really don't make no sense. Because I've been playing tempo, I can remember myself that when, as far as back, that I can remember. I was nothing but a kid. And you know what I used to do? I don't know if you ever saw a song that was kind of a wire that used to go around your neck with a harmonica. Like that. I used to play the harmonica and take my mother's watch stuff. And boy, I was going to town. And I was that small that I couldn't carry the watch stuff. Yeah. That's what I'm saying. There's no such thing if the colored people learn as a temple. Because it's like I'm saying, there's nobody can learn you that. And now, you can believe me when I'm telling you, that the colored people, as far as it's concerned, they're losing more tempo than the white people are doing. Now, pay strictly attention to that now, and I'm going to show you that I'm right about that. I think they rush. I think the drum is rush. Now, right. You're right. Now you come and do it. Sounds to me like they do, but I never say anything. You know why? I'll tell you why. You know why? I'll tell you why. You know why? Dick, I'll tell you why. The changing of the music. In other words. You see, the old time drum players hardly used the sticks on the snare drum with fan brushes. In other words, they were playing with going. No drum solo or nothing. Now, they're taking the drums and going ba dum ba dum ba dum ba dum ba dum ba dum ba dum. See how many kicks they can make on a bass drum. In other words, they're playing a solo drum. They're not playing drums. And there's no man, I don't care who he is, and how fast he is, that he's going to start kicking a drum like that and trying to make too many beats in the measure of the music like that, that he's keeping tempo. He can't do it. I don't care who he is.

I always felt sorry for the bass player in some of these modern jazz bands because he's the only one that's keeping the tempo. The drummer is playing strictly counterpoint, making bombs bursting in air.

That's right. The bass man is the only one making dum ba dum ba dum. And I will say it brought forth the best of the bass. The drum player is making a ribbit. The bum bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing. That's not helping the rhythm at all. Yeah. Oh well. Well, I guess that's it. How were the tempos in the old times? Did they play everything so fast? No, the old tempos was mediocre. That's what I learned. That's mediocre. That's what I want to get into. The same thing. Now the man I spoke to was Sante Piccolo, our trombone player. Well, we came in an argument like that, that to play jazz and to make the people excited or something like that, you've got to play fast. Now, here, now we're going to face something like this. Now we know that everybody, mostly of them anyway, they love Louis because man Louis Armstrong, they think he's the greatest. Okay. We leave it go at that. So now, you take the white bands, even up to Disneyland. Of course, I will say this year, looked like they kind of cooled down a little. But the previous year, everything was... Now that's what they call Dixieland Band. Alright. Well we all play it like that. Understand well. Well as a rule, they put Louis Armstrong as king of jazz. He's the last float to come out the bay. And you know what he's playing? Hello, Dolly. Hello, Dolly. He makes the white bands look cheap. According to the applause that the people has given Louis Armstrong. And I know doing well that the bands that they got out there, it's better than Louis Armstrong has got. But it's just that swing and that tempo, that feeling. In other words, when you play music, you've got to play music where people feel it. It's not that just blah blah blah blah. You've got to play music that the people feel. Now we played over at the famous store. Now Sandra Pecor is playing there and all he's playing there, which I call it, you know, with all respects they're playing there. They're all good musicians and everything. But the tempo they're playing is more ballet house, what they call ballet hall music than anything else. Now we used to play, when we used to play with Shokin, we used to play the right tempo. There's where you can tell the difference of the people, feels it or like it. When we used to play, you see the people take their hands and hit it on the counter. Keep them tempo with the music. If not, it will be a problem. That's what you got to feel. That's what you got to feel. That's what you got to feel. That's what you got to look at. When them people are doing that, they're feeling it. Naturally, if you're playing fast or something, they give you a hand, they know you're trying to do your best and they give you a hand, it's wild. But it's not that they like it, because you're not making them feel it. You understand?
